Free State Election 2021: This Is How Small Towns Die

By: Siniketiwe Hlanze | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Unique Selling Point:
In her recent report the auditor general raised concern that the financial position of municipalities in the Free State province continue to regress and that no council has received a clean audit since 2015/2016. Matjhabeng Municipality, which covers towns like Welkom, Ventersburg and Odendaalsrus, is in a financial free fall with no end in sight. The Municipality owes Sedibeng Water Board R4.1 billion and Eskom over R3 billion, these bills are just a portion of its financial troubles, none of the sewage treatment plants are operational, Telkom has at several times disconnected the council's telephones due to non-payment and its alleged that lifts in the municipal building have been broken for years and there's no money to fix them.

Summary:
The mining industry was the economic bloodline for Welkom, now in its sunset years the closing down of shafts means many people face unemployment and the town loses one of its major financial injections. This place is desperate for new investment but with existing business, from the local tavern, butchery and factories already struggling to operate optimally with no water, electricity and sewage problems, economic prospects dwindle.

Script:


LINK;
I was born here in Thabong, one of the townships that falls under the Matjhabeng municipality here in the Free State.

My grandfather’s house is down this street, he ran a few businesses and had a few taxis. I used to play along here, we had running water, rubbish was collected regularly….coming back here now, and seeing this much litter along the streets truly breaks my heart.
RED - removed repetition going into VO
Kutlwanong brings new meaning to the term waterside property, here effluent runs through the streets, past people’s homes, until it eventually drains into what is now a lush wetland. It’s been this way for years; so long in fact that the stench - so repulsive to outsiders - residents here have simply learnt to live with.
Pulane pointing at marshland, describing the sewage smells, rubbish and snakes….
Pulane Tateri moved to K2 section in Kutlwanong 14 years ago. And every year since, the rainy season has made the stench even worse.
1;47 it’s been a long time, I arrived here and this was already happening. I found people here living under these conditions, a life of struggle, when it rains.
03;05 it smells. You see my little shack, my small shack. If I lock up and go for the whole day, I’ll come back to it smelling. It smells, sometimes, as if you’d left something in there. It’s the sewage, you haven’t left anything, it's the sewage. If you look over that small koppie, it’s all sewage
Nowhere - not the towns, the townships, the farms, the industrial areas - has escaped the impact of a lack of services and the collapse of municipal infrastructure. It’s devastating.

The crippled local municipality scored just 12 - yes, 12 - out of hundred in last year’s financial sustainability index put together by Ratings Afrika. What does that mean? Well, simply put, it has little to no ability to deliver services or maintain infrastructure. Nor does it have the capacity to absorb financial shocks caused by natural factors.

Matjhabeng barely manages to service its debt: it owes a massive R3.7 billion to Eskom, compromising electricity supply. Another example: it owes the Sedibeng Water Board R4 billion and, several days into a complete supply shutdown, a new payment plan had to be signed after the provincial government intervened. Not confident of ever seeing its cash, the water board claims the municipality ducks and dives its commitments.


LINK; Mathjabeng municipality’s money problems culminate in extreme failure of infrastructure, like this waste water treatment plant, which is meant to service the industrial area in welkom and parts of thabong township. There’s clearly been a breakdown here and it seems it’s been like this for a while.
LINK TWEAK OPTION:
This wastewater treatment plant is meant to service the industrial area in Welkom and parts of Thabong township. This is the type of infrastructure that Mathjabeng municipality should be spending resources on, but it’s been broken down for years because there’s simply no money left to pay for its maintenance.
At witpan sewage works...empty reticulation dams...fountain of sewage bursting through pipe




Ratings Afrika analyst, Charl Kocks, says the failure of local municipalities to look after infrastructure has only made their financial position worse.

Charl

08;01
repairs and maintenance on any infrastructure is critical, you can extend the life of a project by 10, 20 even 30 years if you maintain it properly, but if you do not it will collapse and have a much shorter life than what it was designed for.

09;12 yes and remember if this is sanitation related there’s also a process of having that managed on a day to day basis because it’s usually a biological process, if you skip a week, you could find coming back that frankly the system isn’t stable anymore and then it takes weeks to fix. So repairs and maintenance but specifically the management of these plants is critical

Rose Nkhasi, is a town planner and head of the local business chamber. An expert in urban development, she knows this town and surrounding areas better than most.

The infrastructure network on which this area is built hasn’t changed in decades.

It’s old and decaying making maintenance critical.
Rose

03;19 the state of the infrastructure is not very good because of age mainly, because the town was laid out in 1947, so most of it is decaying and the maintenance cost is so big that you can’t just redo the whole town, so it’s done in patches here and there, so it’s not as good as it should be, especially for the growth that the town is seeing at the moment. 04;02 we should be seeing maintenance of infrastructure a lot, because, like I’m saying welkom is old. And being old and the infrastructure struggling to sustain the development on it currently,
So local businesses in Welkom are taking matters into their own hands, fixing municipal pipelines across the city. To keep their doors open, they need this town to work.

Garry Wilson

08;34 yes we supplement water, if there’s a water breakage in the pipeline, we normally have to, they haven’t got spare, so normally what we do, we have to get supplies to get it repaired ourselves. We will supply the valves and the equipment a lot of the times because they havn’t got it for various reasons, obviously the municipality hasn’t got the money to supply the spares to repair, 08;58 so if we don’t do it we haven’t got the water, in this factory here, I’ve got odd of 200 people, they’ve gotta get to toilets ecetera, I can’t live without you know it’s just inhumane….and it doesn’t matter, if we don’t get help, we gotta help ourselves.
Garry Wilson runs five of these heavy engineering plants around town. They need constant water supply. Any leaks and his entire operation is compromised.



And power interruptions? Well that too can trigger expensive losses. Like so many people, he was forced to install a major generator ten years ago to cushion the blow from loadshedding an investment that’s proved to be valuable







04;31 ja look building in welkom, ja there goes the power, so we’re on loadsheding now, must i carry on, can i carry on
Garry Wilson

05;31 the thing is loadshedding you can still plan around, but unfortunately in welkom we have power outages which aren’t planned and that creates chaos.
Like Wilson’s businesses, this beef processing plant can’t escape the impact of service delivery chaos.

Sparta is a familiar brand in Supermarkets, exporting beef across Africa and the middle east.

It’s operations here in Welkom need water and electricity at an industrial scale.


Consider making this part a LINK - ‘Sparta is a familiar brand….

Estelle

00;47
Welkom was actually chosen in those days about 22 years ago because the goldfields, the electricity and water supply was very constant to this area. And that is why we chose to be here. At welkom we process the beef into further cuts we supply about 15 percent of south africa’s beef to all the major super markets and we also export some of our products. To be able to do all of this we require the services at our welkom plant we need eh approximately 1,8 mva of electricity to our plant , we use about 13 thousand kilowatts of electricity per day and we need 1.5 million litters of water to run our operation daily

For CEO, Estelle van Reenen, there are three attributes required of a manager here:to be solutions-driven, brave,and patient. The challenges in Mathjabeng test all three. motto
Estelle
03;27 besides all the everyday problems that you encounter in any business, we have this additional strain on us. But I think we’ve also become like eh cray fish in hot water because we don’t even talk about the daily things we have to do. If you take our staff home at night, we have to do it in four by four vehicles because the condition of the roads are so shocking especially in the middle of the night when you can’t see where you going.
03;59 we have stock in our warehouses of cables and pipes to assist the municipality to perform their services so we can keep our services going. 05;26 so what we have to do is sometimes we have to slaughter our cattle else where at a huge cost and then we some days have to send people home that they can’t come to work cause we can’t continue our operations here. Then if we have water again we have to catch up on weekend days
04;11 and but we don’t even talk about this anymore it’s just everyday business.
But her resilience reserves are starting to run low. Doing business here - especially now - is enough to test anyone’s resolve.

Estelle
07;54 but what is so sad, we’re actually forced now to look at premises elsewhere because we can not be provided more electricity than the 08;16 but we’d hate to go anywhere else, we want to have our business in the free state, you know we’ve had our roots here forever and this is where we want to be.
NEW POTENTIAL LINK: Back in my grandfather’s day, the gold mines were major employers and secondary industries and surrounding farms flourished as a result.
Now in their sunset years, mines are closing
down, leaving unemployment and poverty in their wake.
Welkom’s local economy is in a precarious position.

This mill, much like the abattoir and the steel plant, are important for jobs.

200 men and women at Gristly Mill process grit into different food products like mealie meal, snacks, and livestock feed. It’s an around the clock operation, with about 30 big trucks departing here every day; negotiating roads in a shocking state of disrepair.

But that is not where the challenges end. CEO Arrie reyneke says the constant power interruptions and irregular water supply have pushed operational costs sky high. It’s difficult not to think about eventually giving up, and shutting shop in Welkom.

Arrie
13;44 we are proud south africans, we want to invest in the community and grow not only the country but our town for our kids and the people here but eh at this stage we are, during our director’s meeting and management meeting we are sitting with strategies on a way forward, do we continue, do we further invest in our businesses in welkom as we don’t get the partnership with the local government on the basic services. And that is making it very difficult, we especially on the mill, when we’ve got interruptions, lets say water interruptions, electricity interruptions due to vandalism of sub stations, on the mill alone we lose about a hundred thousand rand per hour on no production. 15;53 and then you get to a certain stage where you ask yourself, is it worth your while to go into this process but you don’t get the assistance or partnership of your local government

15;19 and I think it’s a very sad question because we are proud, a lot of us, a lot of the people were born in welkom, grown up in welkom, involved in the schools in the churches, so, welkom I think 15;59 I just think it’s, it’s not fair, I think it’s not fair to the people that are working here.

For many in this town, basic services are already beyond their reach. Driven to poverty by a lack of work. And as opportunities continue to shrink, their number only grows.

Charl Kocks says most municipalities in the Free State can barely collect the revenue they need to supply services. Yet, astonishingly, budgets based on a hundred percent collection rates are drawn up and approved… despite being utterly unrealistic.




john.webb@giantmedia.orgthis is the actual comment - took out “Charl Kock says” - back in now.

Charl
06;06 sadly and remember we don’t cover all municipalities in the Free state we only cover nine, not one single municipality of all that we cover is even getting 35 percent, which is kind of minimal survival level, it’s not sustainable, sustainable is 50 and up, but not any of those municipalities are getting close to that. We’re talking 11 percent, 11.9, 20.8, let’s give it big numbers 12, 21, 16, 18, 12, 13 16 15 31. These are not survival numbers. 06;45 the highest ranking number in the free state is 31 out of a hundred, the third highest is 18 06;59 matjhabeng is below that, just under 12. 07;06 it is frightening and let me make it clear we set up the mfsi to try and help municipalities to improve these things hurst us in a very significant way, we feel for south Africa, because at every level this is where people live and where people are not being serviced because the municipality can’t anymore.
With an unrealistic budget compounded by astronomical debt and dismal audit outcomes in the last financial year - Matjhabeng was one of the country’s highest contributors to wasteful and fruitless expenditure, at close to a billion rand. Unauthorised expenditure - another key financial red flag - breached the one billion rand mark.

Desperate to see Welkom work means constantly engaging the municipality on behalf of business. Even lobbying for posts to be filled by qualified people.
Rose
07;54 Rose- most businesses are trying their best to stay in welkom, we, mining is declining, and we are competing with areas like Rustenburg where a lot of eh mining related businesses are moving to. So we’re trying to work on things that can, incentives, that can keep them here or even try and attract some to come into the area that’s why we’re trying to sort out our infrastructure issues so that we don’t even lose more businesses like the ones we’re seeing because it’s becoming more expensive to live in our area.

If you’ve watched the carte blanche election roadshow you’ll know rustenburg is hardly a shining example of municipal efficiency that business here in welkom are considering moving there tells it’s own story





PROMOS

Municipalities across the Free State can barely deliver services and small towns are buckling under the pressure of unemployment and poverty, what will be left behind once businesses pack up and leave

Pipelines in Welkom are old and decaying, with no money to maintain infrastructure, businesses are stepping in where the Matjhabeng municipality is failing and it comes at a high cost. Estelle 03;59 we have stock in our warehouses of cables and pipes to assist the municipality to perform their services so we can keep our services going.

Matjhabeng municipality’s money problems run deep and it’s the businesses and communities that pay the price for the council’s mismanagement. Garry Wilson 05;31 the thing is loadshedding you can still plan around, but unfortunately in welkom we have power outages which aren’t planned and that creates chaos.

metadata.Unique Selling Point: In her recent report the auditor general raised concern that the financial position of municipalities in the Free State province continue to regress and that no council has received a clean audit since 2015/2016. Matjhabeng Municipality, which covers towns like Welkom, Ventersburg and Odendaalsrus, is in a financial free fall with no end in sight. The Municipality owes Sedibeng Water Board R4.1 billion and Eskom over R3 billion, these bills are just a portion of its financial troubles, none of the sewage treatment plants are operational, Telkom has at several times disconnected the council's telephones due to non-payment and its alleged that lifts in the municipal building have been broken for years and there's no money to fix them.
metadata.Summary: The mining industry was the economic bloodline for Welkom, now in its sunset years the closing down of shafts means many people face unemployment and the town loses one of its major financial injections. This place is desperate for new investment but with existing business, from the local tavern, butchery and factories already struggling to operate optimally with no water, electricity and sewage problems, economic prospects dwindle.
